title: How to Improve Decision Making in Football (Player Guide)

ops.anchor: and review your own decisions after each match.
ops.html:
Key takeaways

  • Most "bad decisions" are late pictures: you looked too late, so you only saw one option.
  • Use the same 3 steps every time: look before the ball arrives, compare forward, keep or change, then commit.
  • The right choice comes from the picture. The same pass can be right in one moment and wrong in the next.
  • You can train the reading part alone with match situations, focused match watching and a short review after each game.
  • At team training, game-like practice such as rondos and small-sided games builds decisions better than repeating one drill.

ops.anchor: Why you make the wrong decision
ops.html:
What is decision making in football?

Decision making in football is choosing what to do, with or without the ball, from what you see around you, fast enough for the action to still work. It has three parts: seeing the picture, picking an option, and carrying it out with the right technique. A mistake in any of the three looks like a "bad decision".

The FA's Boot Room describes it as "the art of choosing a particular technique, action, or tactic which is of benefit to the team". The table shows where each part usually goes wrong and how to train it.

PartWhat happensWhat goes wrongHow to train it
1. SeeYou look around and notice pressure, free teammates and spaceYou only watch the ball, so the defender behind you is a surpriseScanning drills and the scanning test
2. ChooseYou compare two or three options for that pictureYou take your first idea, or freeze between twoMatch situations, and watching games with pause-and-predict
3. DoYou play the pass, take the touch or make the runRight idea, poor pass or heavy touchTechnique under pressure: rondos, wall work with a time limit

How to get more decisions out of team training

Game-like practice builds decision making better than repeating the same drill, so get the most out of rondos, small-sided games and match play. You can add your own hidden rules that nobody else needs to know about: look before every touch, know your next pass before the ball arrives, and pick the forward option whenever it is on.

  • Rondos: check a shoulder before each touch and know where your next pass goes before you receive. Two touches at most.
  • Small-sided games: try to receive half-turned, facing forward, and count how many times you play forward when it is on.
  • Passing patterns with no opponents: these train technique, not decisions. Add a look over your shoulder before every pass so they train something extra.
  • After the session: ask your coach about one moment: "What was the better option there?" Asking about what you saw is part of how decision-makers develop, as the FA's Boot Room piece points out for coaches.
  • Matches: pick one decision to focus on for the whole game, like when to take your full-back on, and review it afterwards.

Coaches call extra rules like these "constraints". They change what the game asks of you without stopping it, which is why they work better than being told what to do.

faq_add.q: What is decision making in football?
faq_add.a: Decision making in football is choosing the best action for what is happening around you, fast enough for it to still work. It depends on seeing the picture early, comparing your options and carrying out your choice with good technique.

faq_add.q: How do I stop hesitating on the ball?
faq_add.a: Decide your first option before the ball arrives and keep one backup ready. Hesitation usually means you are still looking when the ball lands. Then commit fully, because a decent option done with conviction usually beats a better one done halfway.

faq_add.q: What drills improve decision making in football?
faq_add.a: Drills with live opponents and real choices work best: rondos, small-sided games and 2v1s. Passing patterns with no opponents train technique, not decisions. Alone, work through match situations, watch games with pause-and-predict and do wall passes with a shoulder check.

faq_add.q: Can decision making in football be trained?
faq_add.a: Yes. Seeing the picture and recognising common situations both improve with practice. A 2022 review found video-based training improved anticipation or decision-making test results in 8 of 10 studies, though the studies were set up differently, so treat it as promising, not proven.
